card.display_name: Strategy A - Semis Breadth-Capped Rotation · ranked by stretch in ATR units
card.thesis: This engine cannot express relative strength: entry and exit are evaluated per symbol against that symbol's own bars, with no cross-sectional comparison, so there is no way to buy 'the strongest semiconductor name' or trade a spread. What this card actually does is apply one absolute condition -- close above its own 50-day average with RSI(14) between 55 and 80, i.e. a confirmed, non-extreme uptrend -- identically to a 9-name cyclical-semiconductor universe (NVDA AMD MU INTC MRVL AVGO TSM QCOM SOXX), and cap concurrent holdings at 3 of 9. That cap is the only 'rotation' logic available: the mechanism is that semiconductor demand and AI-capex cycles tend to move the whole group together and to persist for quarters rather than days, so entering only into names already confirmed in trend, and exiting on trend break or momentum fade, should keep capital on the right side of the cycle more often than not, while the cap prevents any single session from committing to more than 3 names at once. I measured pairwise daily-return correlation across these 9 names over the trailing ~253 sessions through 2026-02-13: mean 0.589, range 0.286 (INTC vs AVGO) to 0.824 (SOXX vs TSM). That is high -- this is a concentrated sector bet dressed as a 3-of-9 rotation, not a diversified basket, and I am not pretending otherwise. It is not a coin-flip between one name and nothing, though: breadth genuinely varies session to session under the proposed filter (median 4 of 9 names qualifying; at least 4 qualify on 50.6% of sessions, at least 6 on 21.3%), so the cap binds and actually forces a choice often enough to matter. When more than 3 names qualify on the same session, the broker fills entries in the fixed order the universe list is written -- alphabetical here -- not by any measure of relative strength, momentum magnitude, or liquidity. That is an arbitrary tiebreak, not a 'buy the leader' mechanism, and the card cannot do better than that. On the other side of these trades: momentum/trend traders who initiated the move earlier and are already positioned before this rule confirms it; mean-reversion sellers who fade strength too early inside a still-intact uptrend and get run over; and dip-buyers in choppy or declining regimes who buy bottoms this rule cannot see coming and will instead get chopped by.
card.entry: close > sma(50) and rsi(14) > 55 and rsi(14) < 80

card.display_name: C21 - Uncorrelated: global macro trend across commodities, precious metals and EM equities
card.thesis: This card exists to be the leg of the combined book that does not move with B-momentum or C-trend, which trade the AI/semis capex cycle through NVDA/AVGO/TSM/META-type names. My universe -- DBC, USO, GDX, FXI, EWZ, SLV -- is priced by six different demand mechanisms with nothing to do with AI capex: global commodity supply/demand and inflation expectations (DBC, USO), monetary/safe-haven demand for precious metals plus mining-equity operating leverage (GDX, SLV), and two single-country equity markets whose dominant drivers are domestic policy and currency, not US tech earnings (FXI: China regulatory and property cycle; EWZ: Brazil commodity-and-political cycle). Measured over the trailing two years through 2026-02-13, daily-return correlation of each name to an equal-weighted composite of B-momentum's 12 tickers is 0.21-0.34 (DBC 0.268, USO 0.213, GDX 0.237, FXI 0.334, EWZ 0.338; SLV in the same 0.2-0.3 band) -- all well below the B-momentum/C-trend pairing this round measured at +0.57, and well below EEM (0.655), EFA (0.594) and HYG (0.563), which I tested and rejected precisely because they still smuggle in AI-heavy Taiwan/Korea tech (EEM/EFA both hold TSM-adjacent exposure) or equity risk-on credit beta (HYG). The counterparty on my trades is whoever is positioned for a US-tech-specific cycle and is surprised by an oil supply shock, a Fed tightening surprise that moves EM currencies, or a China policy shift -- none of which shows up in an NVDA earnings call. Unlike c14's TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD, which is duration-only and was flagged as idle 55 straight live sessions because close>sma(150) rejected all four correlated bond/gold names at once, this basket's six legs are only moderately correlated with each other (they are driven by oil, gold, China policy and Brazil politics separately), so over the trailing 90 sessions through cutoff at least one name was in its close>sma(100) regime on every single session (avg 4.7 of 6 names simultaneously), with zero idle days -- the diversification that keeps correlation to B-momentum low is the same diversification that keeps this card from ever going fully dark. Entry: close>sma(100) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30) -- a faster regime filter than c14's sma(150) and no RSI overbought gate, chosen specifically to raise firing frequency rather than restrict it, since beating c14's idle-desk problem is this card's second job. Exit is the symmetric ema(10) crosses_below ema(30), backstopped by a 15% stop (matched to this basket's 14-37% annualized vol, well above bonds but below single growth stocks) and a 150-day time stop. Measured buy-and-hold evidence in the two windows built to be adversarial to a duration hedge: taper-2013, where TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD fell 0.2% to -11.7%, this basket averaged roughly flat (+0.1%, oil's own supply rally offsetting EWZ's EM sell-off); inflation-2021, where c14's basket was uniformly negative (-3.6% to -6.2%), this basket averaged roughly +6% on commodities' inflation rally offsetting weak gold miners and EM equities. Falsification: if this basket's daily correlation to B-momentum rises materially above the measured 0.2-0.35 band once trading windows include a genuine global risk-off event (all risk assets, including commodities and EM, selling off in the same session as AI names), or if the six legs stop diversifying each other's regime timing and start entering/exiting together the way c14's four did, the uncorrelated-leg thesis is wrong, not just underperforming.
card.entry: close > sma(100) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30)

card.display_name: C19 - Panic-Bid: financials/energy shock reversion · ranked by relative strength
card.thesis: A close below the 20-day, 2-sigma Bollinger lower band, with RSI(14) under 30 and the day's true range exceeding its own 14-day ATR, is three independent confirmations of the same event: a statistically extreme, accelerating one-day dislocation, not an ordinary pullback inside a trend. In financials and energy specifically -- the two sectors whose largest single-day moves have repeatedly been forced selling rather than a revision of fundamentals (margin calls, fund redemptions, program-driven de-grossing, a headline that gets re-priced within days once it is understood) -- that kind of move tends to partially retrace over the following one to three weeks, because the sellers on the shock day are disproportionately non-economic: risk desks cutting exposure into a VaR breach, index/ETF-driven flows, and retail panic, not new information about ten years of future cash flows for JPMorgan or Exxon. The counterparty on the other side of my buy is exactly that forced seller -- someone selling because a risk limit or a margin call requires it that day, not because they have re-underwritten the business -- and the person I hand the position to on exit is whoever is chasing the bounce once the panic is visibly over. This is a volatility-discipline entry, not a dip-buy dressed up as one: the ATR-relative range condition is what is missing from a plain RSI/Bollinger mean-reversion rule, and it is what keeps the trigger anchored to days when the market is repricing fast rather than merely drifting to an oversold reading over two quiet weeks. The strategy is a genuine short-vol / mean-reversion payoff, not a convex one: it harvests a moderate, capped reversion after each shock and is capped on the downside by a stop, but a stop checked against the prior close (not the intraday low, per the engine's execution model) means a shock that is the start of a structural decline rather than a one-day panic -- oil in the second half of 2014 is the clearest historical case in this universe -- can gap through the stop before it is caught, which is this strategy's real tail risk and is stated here before any result exists, not fitted after seeing one.
card.entry: close < bb_lower(20,2) and rsi(14) < 30 and high - low > atr(14)
